disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by the presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both, which are time-consuming or cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Obsessions are recurrent, intrusive thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as unwanted and typically generate marked anxiety or disgust, while compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce this distress or prevent a feared event, despite being excessive or not realistically connected. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood and tends to follow a chronic, waxing-and-waning course, frequently exacerbated by stress, responsibility increases, or role transitions. It is distinguished from related conditions such as generalized anxiety disorder (more free-floating worry), psychotic disorders (lack of insight, delusional conviction), and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (ego-syntonic perfectionism without intrusive thoughts) by the ego-dystonic, intrusive nature of obsessions and the ritualistic responses to them.

narrative.personality: Kevin is a meticulous, reliability-focused technician who enjoys complex technical challenges, outdoor adventures, and creative hobbies like photography and music, and tends to push himself hard to get every detail right.
narrative.stressor: Kevin traces the start of his difficulties to a period two years ago when his station underwent a major rebrand and he was promoted, informally, to be the de facto lead on several high-stakes live broadcasts. The new role meant longer hours, tighter timelines, and a sense that any technical mistake on his part would be visible to thousands of viewers and could jeopardize his reputation and team. As he took on designing system upgrades and supervising more junior staff, he found himself increasingly preoccupied with the possibility of catastrophic failures, replaying worst-case scenarios in his mind even during his off hours and on weekend hikes. Over time this constant mental checking and second-guessing began to slow his work, cut into his sleep as he stayed up re-reviewing setups and documentation, and caused friction at home when his spouse noticed he was mentally “still at the studio,” which finally led him to seek psychiatric help when he realized he could no longer trust himself to stop these thoughts on his own.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting these intrusive thoughts about things going wrong at work, and I can’t switch them off no matter how much I tell myself everything’s fine.”

narrative.personality: Acacia is a sociable, routine-loving, hands-on worker who takes pride in craftsmanship and community involvement, often saying yes to others and juggling many commitments with an upbeat attitude.
narrative.stressor: Acacia’s problems intensified after a major restructuring at the plant about three years ago, when several experienced coworkers were laid off and she was asked to take on additional quality-control responsibilities while also training a wave of new hires. At the same time, her teenage children became more independent, and she responded by pouring even more of herself into church activities, community events, and baking for every gathering, leaving her stretched thin and anxious about letting anyone down. With fewer trusted colleagues to double-check her work and more eyes on her as a trainer and mediator, she began to feel personally responsible for catching every possible defect and for keeping the line “perfect,” extending this sense of responsibility into her home life and volunteer roles. As her routines to reassure herself that nothing was missed grew longer and more rigid, she started falling behind at work, coming in early and staying late, and missing social plans, which alarmed her family and eventually prompted her to agree to an evaluation when her supervisor gently suggested she might need support.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve gotten into these rigid routines I feel I have to do over and over or I can’t relax, and they’re starting to take over my day.”

narrative.personality: Mesha is a detail-oriented, creative, and somewhat anxious person who channels their competitiveness into work performance and artistic pursuits, often overthinking situations and striving to do everything just right.
narrative.stressor: Mesha reports that her difficulties began subtly after she and her spouse had a series of conflicts about finances and the decision to postpone having children, which left her feeling guilty, uncertain about the future, and worried about being perceived as selfish or irresponsible. Around the same time, a minor till discrepancy at work—quickly resolved and not her fault—shook her confidence in her own attention to detail, something she prided herself on. These events seemed to tap into longstanding insecurities, and she started spending more and more mental energy revisiting conversations with her spouse and minor interactions with customers, questioning what they really meant and whether she might have inadvertently done something terrible. Over months, this constant mental replaying and self-interrogation began to intrude on her drawing time, her ability to focus at the register, and even her enjoyment of book club, leading her to seek psychiatric help when she noticed she could no longer control where her mind went and feared it might cost her both her job and her marriage.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My head is constantly filled with unwanted, disturbing what-if thoughts that I can’t shut off, even when I know they don’t make sense.”
